item.title: How Rising and Falling Costs Distort Inventory Numbers
item.summary: When the price of inventory moves over time, the cost method a company picks (FIFO, LIFO or weighted average) changes its profit, inventory, taxes and ratios, even though the business itself is unchanged. This lesson shows the direction of each effect in inflation and deflation, and how to restate a LIFO company onto a FIFO basis so you can compare it with peers.

sections.heading: Same shelf, different price tags
sections.body_markdown:
A shop buys the same item several times in a year at different prices. When it sells one, accounting has to decide **which purchase price** moves from the balance sheet (inventory) to the income statement (**cost of goods sold, COGS**, the cost of items sold). That decision is the **cost flow assumption**.

- **FIFO (first-in, first-out)**: the oldest costs go to COGS first; the newest costs stay in inventory.
- **LIFO (last-in, first-out)**: the newest costs go to COGS first; the oldest costs stay in inventory.
- **Weighted average**: every unit gets the average cost of all goods available, so the result sits between FIFO and LIFO.

Think of a stack of towels in a cupboard. FIFO takes from the bottom (old towels) and leaves the newest on top. LIFO takes from the top and leaves the oldest at the bottom, possibly for years.

The physical goods are identical under every method. Only the accounting label on them changes. Gross profit is sales minus COGS, so whichever cost lands in COGS drives gross profit and, after expenses and tax, net income.

sections.heading: Inflation versus deflation: who gets the old cost?
sections.body_markdown:
**Rising costs (inflation).** The oldest cost is the cheapest and the newest is the dearest.

- **FIFO**: cheap old costs go to COGS, so COGS is *lower*, gross profit and net income are *higher*, and ending inventory holds the newest costs, so it is close to current cost. Income tax is higher.
- **LIFO**: dear new costs go to COGS, so COGS is *higher*, profit is *lower*, income tax is lower, and ending inventory holds old cheap costs, so it is *below* current cost.
- **Weighted average**: in between on every measure.

**Falling costs (deflation).** Everything flips, because now the oldest cost is the dearest.

- **FIFO**: dear old costs go to COGS, so COGS is higher, profit is *lower*, and ending inventory is at the newest (low) costs.
- **LIFO**: cheap new costs go to COGS, so COGS is lower, profit is *higher*, and ending inventory still carries old, dear costs, so it is *above* current cost.
- **Weighted average**: again in between.

A quick memory rule: **the method that sends the higher cost to COGS reports the lower profit and the lower inventory.** Ask first whether the newest cost is higher or lower than the oldest, then decide which method sends it to COGS.

(Write-downs of inventory to net realisable value are a separate topic and are not covered here.)

Under U.S. rules, a company that uses LIFO for tax generally must also use it in its reported statements (the LIFO conformity rule). This is a big reason LIFO is common in industries with persistent price increases. IFRS (IAS 2) does not permit LIFO at all.

sections.heading: What it does to ratios
sections.body_markdown:
Suppose costs are rising and inventory quantities are steady. Compared with an otherwise identical FIFO company, the LIFO company shows:

- **Lower gross margin and net margin** (higher COGS).
- **Lower current ratio** (current assets / current liabilities), because inventory in current assets is smaller.
- **Higher inventory turnover** ($\text{COGS} / \text{average inventory}$): the numerator is bigger and the denominator is smaller. Days of inventory on hand are correspondingly *shorter*.
- **Higher debt-to-equity**, because lower cumulative profits mean lower equity.
- **Lower reported taxes**, so more cash stays in the business (where LIFO is allowed for tax).

The better turnover is a **bookkeeping effect, not better efficiency**. The two companies could be identical in reality. In deflation the signs reverse: LIFO shows higher margins and a higher current ratio, and FIFO shows the higher turnover.

This is why an analyst cannot compare a LIFO firm with a FIFO firm directly. First put both on the same basis.

sections.heading: Restating LIFO onto FIFO with the LIFO reserve
sections.body_markdown:
LIFO companies disclose a **LIFO reserve**: the amount by which FIFO (roughly current-cost) inventory exceeds LIFO inventory.

$$\text{LIFO reserve}=\text{Inventory}_{FIFO}-\text{Inventory}_{LIFO}$$

**Balance sheet:** add the reserve to LIFO inventory to get FIFO inventory.

**Income statement:** if the reserve grew during the year, FIFO COGS was lower than LIFO COGS by exactly that growth:

$$\text{COGS}_{FIFO}=\text{COGS}_{LIFO}-(\text{Reserve}_{end}-\text{Reserve}_{begin})$$

A lower COGS raises pre-tax income by the same amount. Net income rises by the change in reserve times $(1-t)$.

**Equity:** the cumulative extra profit is the whole reserve, but tax would have been paid on it, so equity (retained earnings) rises by $\text{Reserve}_{end}\times(1-t)$. The remaining $\text{Reserve}_{end}\times t$ is the extra tax liability.

If the reserve **shrinks** (falling costs, or shrinking inventory quantity), the change is negative and FIFO COGS ends up *higher* than LIFO COGS. After restating, recompute margins, current ratio, turnover and debt-to-equity and compare.

sections.heading: LIFO liquidation: when old costs leak out
sections.body_markdown:
If a LIFO company sells more units than it buys, it digs into its old bottom layers of inventory. During inflation those layers are cheap, so cheap old costs are matched against today's sales revenue. COGS drops, and gross profit and net income jump.

This is a **LIFO liquidation**. The extra profit is a one-off accounting effect, not a sign of better operations. Because it can flatter results, companies disclose it in their notes, and analysts strip it out when judging how sustainable earnings are. Liquidation also pulls down the LIFO reserve, which is one clue that it may have happened.

worked_example.problem: A company uses LIFO. For the year it reports sales of $3,200, LIFO COGS of $2,000 and year-end LIFO inventory of $600 (all in thousands). Its LIFO reserve was $120 at the start of the year and $150 at the end. The tax rate is 25%. Restate to FIFO: find inventory, COGS, gross profit and gross margin, the change in net income, and the change in equity.
steps: FIFO inventory = LIFO inventory + ending reserve = 600 + 150 = 750. Keys: 600 [+] 150 [=] → 750.
Change in reserve = 150 − 120 = 30 (the reserve rose, which is consistent with rising costs).
FIFO COGS = LIFO COGS − change in reserve = 2,000 − 30 = 1,970. Keys: 2000 [−] 30 [=] → 1,970.
Net income rises by the change in reserve after tax: 30 × (1 − 0.25) = 22.5. Keys: 30 [×] 0.75 [=] → 22.5.
Equity rises by the whole ending reserve after tax: 150 × 0.75 = 112.5. The extra tax liability is 150 × 0.25 = 37.5.
worked_example.answer: On a FIFO basis: inventory $750, COGS $1,970, gross profit $1,230 (gross margin about 38.4% versus 37.5% under LIFO), net income higher by $22.5, and equity higher by $112.5 (all in thousands).

formulas.name: LIFO reserve
formulas.where: Inv_FIFO is inventory on a FIFO basis; Inv_LIFO is inventory as reported under LIFO.

formulas.name: FIFO inventory from LIFO
formulas.where: Reserve_end is the LIFO reserve at the balance sheet date.

formulas.name: FIFO COGS from LIFO
formulas.where: COGS_LIFO is reported cost of goods sold; Reserve_begin and Reserve_end are the LIFO reserve at the start and end of the year.

formulas.name: After-tax adjustment to net income and equity
formulas.where: ΔReserve is the change in the reserve over the year; t is the tax rate as a decimal; Reserve_end is the ending reserve.

formulas.name: Inventory turnover
formulas.where: COGS is cost of goods sold for the period; average inventory is usually (beginning + ending inventory) / 2.

exam_traps: Assuming LIFO always lowers income. That is true only when costs are rising; in deflation LIFO reports higher income and FIFO lower.
Getting the sign wrong on the COGS restatement: FIFO COGS = LIFO COGS minus the *increase* in the reserve, not plus it and not minus the whole ending reserve.
Forgetting tax on the equity adjustment: equity rises by the ending reserve × (1 − t), while the inventory adjustment is the full reserve (the tax part shows up as extra liability).
Treating LIFO's higher inventory turnover as evidence of better efficiency, when it is just higher COGS over lower inventory.
Treating weighted average as an extreme method. It always falls between FIFO and LIFO, in both inflation and deflation.
Missing that a shrinking reserve or inventory decline under LIFO in inflation may signal a LIFO liquidation that inflates profit.

item.stem: Purchase costs rise throughout the year, and year-end inventory quantities equal those at the start of the year. Compared with an otherwise identical company using FIFO, a company using LIFO reports:

options.text: Higher COGS, lower net income, and lower ending inventory.
options.explanation: Correct. LIFO expenses the newest, dearest costs first, so COGS is higher and profit lower. The older, cheaper costs stay in inventory, so ending inventory is lower.

options.text: Lower COGS, higher net income, and lower ending inventory.
options.explanation: Mixes up the methods. Lower COGS and higher income are FIFO effects in inflation. LIFO does not lower COGS when costs are rising.

options.text: Higher COGS, lower net income, and higher ending inventory.
options.explanation: Gets the income effect right but assumes LIFO leaves the newest, dear costs in inventory. LIFO leaves the oldest, cheapest layers there, so inventory is lower.

item.stem: Purchase costs fall steadily during the year, and inventory quantities never drop below their opening level. Sales and all other expenses are identical across methods. Which method reports the highest net income?

options.explanation: Applies the inflation rule (FIFO = highest income). With falling costs FIFO expenses the oldest, dearest costs first, so it gives the lowest income.
Weighted average sits between FIFO and LIFO. It is never the highest or lowest when costs move in one direction.
Correct. LIFO sends the newest, cheapest costs to COGS, so COGS is lowest and net income highest when costs are falling.

item.stem: A retailer buys four units of a product, one unit per purchase, at $40, $44, $46 and $50 in that order (costs are rising). Using the periodic weighted-average method, what cost per unit is assigned to a unit sold? Answer to the nearest dollar.

options.explanation: This is the FIFO cost (the oldest purchase). Weighted average blends all four purchases rather than using the first one.
Correct. With equal quantities in each purchase, the weighted average is the simple average: (40 + 44 + 46 + 50) / 4 = 180 / 4 = 45. It lies between the FIFO and LIFO costs.
This is the LIFO cost (the newest purchase). Weighted average does not use only the latest cost.

item.stem: A company reports LIFO inventory of $850 (thousand) and discloses a LIFO reserve of $210 (thousand). The tax rate is 30%. What is inventory on a FIFO basis?

options.explanation: Subtracts the reserve from LIFO inventory. FIFO inventory is higher than LIFO when costs have risen, so the reserve must be added.
Adds the reserve after tax (850 + 210 × 0.7). The tax effect belongs in equity and liabilities, not in the inventory adjustment, which uses the full reserve.
Correct. FIFO inventory = LIFO inventory + LIFO reserve = 850 + 210 = 1,060.

item.stem: A LIFO company reports COGS of $5,400 (thousand). Its LIFO reserve was $300 thousand at the start of the year and $380 thousand at the end. What is COGS on a FIFO basis?

options.explanation: Correct. The reserve rose by 380 − 300 = 80, so FIFO COGS is lower: 5,400 − 80 = 5,320.
Adds the change in reserve instead of subtracting it. When costs rise, FIFO COGS is lower than LIFO COGS.
Subtracts the whole ending reserve (380) instead of only the change over the year. The cumulative reserve belongs on the balance sheet; COGS reflects only this year's change.

item.stem: Purchase costs are rising and inventory quantities are stable. Two otherwise identical companies have the same sales, purchases and current liabilities. One uses FIFO and the other uses LIFO. Ignore any difference in cash caused by income taxes. Inventory turnover is cost of goods sold divided by average inventory. Compared with the FIFO company, the LIFO company's current ratio and inventory turnover will typically be:

options.text: A higher current ratio and a lower inventory turnover
options.explanation: This reverses both effects. Under rising costs LIFO reports lower inventory, which reduces current assets and the current ratio. LIFO also reports higher COGS, which raises turnover.

options.text: A lower current ratio and a higher inventory turnover
options.explanation: Correct. LIFO leaves the older, cheaper costs in ending inventory, so reported inventory and current assets are lower and the current ratio falls. LIFO charges the newest, higher costs to COGS, so COGS is higher. Turnover is higher COGS divided by a smaller average inventory, so it rises.

options.text: A lower current ratio and a lower inventory turnover
options.explanation: The current ratio is right, but the turnover is wrong. This option assumes that lower reported profit means lower turnover. Turnover uses COGS, which is higher under LIFO, divided by a smaller inventory, so it is higher.

issues: solver chose C (high): LIFO carries lower inventory, so the current ratio is lower. Its COGS is higher and its average inventory is lower, so inventory turnover is higher. Option B states this combination, which is the correct pairing, so the index points to B.}

item.stem: In a period of rising costs, a LIFO company sells more units than it buys, so its inventory quantity falls and a LIFO liquidation occurs. What is the most likely effect on reported results?

options.text: COGS rises sharply because the newest, dearest costs are expensed first.
options.explanation: That is ordinary LIFO behaviour, not the liquidation effect. In a liquidation, the layers reaching COGS are the old ones.

options.text: Net income falls because old costs are revalued to current cost.
options.explanation: LIFO layers are not revalued. Old costs stay at their original amounts and simply move to COGS.

options.text: Gross margin is boosted because older, lower costs flow into COGS.
options.explanation: Correct. Cheap old layers are matched against current-price sales, lowering COGS and temporarily inflating gross profit and net income.

item.stem: A LIFO company has an ending LIFO reserve of $210 thousand and a tax rate of 30%. By how much does shareholders' equity increase when the statements are restated to FIFO?

options.explanation: This is only the tax portion (210 × 0.30), which becomes an extra tax liability, not the equity increase.
Correct. The cumulative extra profit is the reserve, but tax would have been paid on it: 210 × (1 − 0.30) = 147.
Ignores the tax effect. The full reserve adjusts inventory, but equity rises only by the after-tax amount.

item.front: When purchase costs are rising, how do LIFO results compare with FIFO (COGS, net income, ending inventory)?
item.back: LIFO has higher COGS, lower net income and lower ending inventory, because the newest, dearest costs are expensed and the oldest, cheapest stay in inventory. Weighted average falls in between.

item.front: What happens to the FIFO vs LIFO comparison when costs fall (deflation)?
item.back: It reverses. FIFO gives higher COGS, lower net income and lower inventory. LIFO gives lower COGS, higher net income and inventory that includes older, dearer costs.

item.front: How do you convert LIFO COGS to FIFO COGS using the LIFO reserve?
item.back: COGS(FIFO) = COGS(LIFO) − (ending reserve − beginning reserve). A rising reserve means FIFO COGS is lower.

item.front: By how much do FIFO inventory and equity exceed the LIFO figures, given a LIFO reserve and tax rate t?
item.back: Inventory is higher by the full reserve; equity is higher by reserve × (1 − t). The reserve × t part is an extra tax liability.

item.front: What is a LIFO liquidation and why do analysts care?
item.back: It is when LIFO inventory quantity falls so that old, usually cheaper, cost layers hit COGS. In inflation this temporarily inflates gross profit and net income, so analysts adjust for it.
